speaker: gm
text:
Behind the King's Granary, a grey-coated clerk turns slowly from the sack hoist above the shut loft door. A pigeon occupies the beam with the settled air of a tenant whose lease predates the building. Below, a scrawny boy in enormous black boots lobs gutter stones at the body. “Cob’s got better aim than the bleedin’ watch!” A sharp-faced girl on the wall top answers in two languages, both uncomplimentary.

A woman in a rain cape steps away from the open gate, notebook in hand. “Sergeant Agnes Kell. The Captain says suicide. I haven’t written that down.” The boy’s next stone strikes the hoist hook with a sharp clang. The pigeon takes this as a criticism of its management and flies.

marks.note: Granary rats are children who run errands and sleep rough around the yards; porters chase them off, and the watch can take them to the Mending House.
Kell is known for recording what happened, not simply accepting the Captain’s account. The Captain has called Prout’s death suicide, but she hasn’t recorded that as fact.

speaker: player
text: Sergeant Kell. Aurelian Thorne, at the King's request. Good — an unwritten verdict is the only kind worth having at this hour. (I raise a hand toward the boy without looking at him) You, with the boots: one more stone at that body and I shall make your boots dance off without you. (Then, to Kell) Who found him, when, and has anyone touched the rope?

speaker: gm
text:
Kell gives you a short nod. “The porters found him at first light. The palace reported him missing last night. No one’s touched the rope. They couldn’t reach it.”

Your raised hand doesn’t stop Cob’s next stone. It strikes the cobbles short of Prout, and the boy looks up at you, suddenly less cocky. “Cob’s boots dance when Cob says they do.” He stamps once; the left boot gives a faint crackle.

The girl on the wall stops drumming her heels. “Threaten him again, silk-ears, and see how far you get.” Kell’s pencil taps once against her notebook. “The boots are the deceased’s, then?” she asks, watching the boy.

speaker: player
text: (I look Prout up and down — feet first) Observe, Sergeant: our clerk hangs in his stockings. A man does not climb to a hoist beam barefoot and then kick his boots to the gutter. (To the boy, more mildly) Cob, is it? Those boots crackle. There's paper in the left one. I'll trade you a silver crown for the boots and whatever's in them — which is more than a dead man's footwear has ever fetched.

speaker: gm
text:
Kell follows your look to the stockinged feet, then makes a brief note. “Stockings, not boots. Noted.” The pencil pauses at your conclusion. “That’s a theory, investigator. I can’t arrest a theory.”

Cob stops throwing stones. At the mention of the left boot, his shoulders tighten; then he leans back into the swagger. “A silver crown? For a look? Cob’s boots are worth two. Each. And that’s before the crackly bit.” He stamps the left one, the leather gives its small crackle, and he folds his arms around his knees. “Pay first, silk-ears. Boot stays on.” The girl on the wall watches his face, not yours.

speaker: player
text: (I flip one silver crown so it spins in the air and lands on the cobbles at Cob's feet) Half now, as a show of good faith. The other crown when the paper is in my hand — the boots you may keep; I've no wish to wear them. (I glance up at the girl on the wall) And you, who watches his face rather than mine: you're the clever one. Were you two here when he was strung up, or merely first to the plunder?

speaker: gm
text:
The crown spins down and comes to rest by Cob’s oversized boot. He snatches it up. For a moment, he studies the shine; then his chin comes up.

“That’s half a crown, silk-ears. You said a crown for the boots and the crackly bit. Cob heard you. Cob’s keeping the boots.”

He curls his fist around the coin and stamps the left boot. It crackles faintly. “And the other half’s a crown more. For a look. No picking, no pulling, no taking. Cob’s not some bleedin’ market turnip.”

The girl’s gaze stays on him. “We were here at first light, weren’t we? You asking who got there first, or who did the stringing?”

marks.note: You offered a silver crown for the boots and whatever was inside; now Cob is holding you to that bargain while keeping the boots.
You offered to pay for a look at the paper, but Cob is setting the terms: he’ll keep the boots and won’t let you handle their contents.

speaker: player
text: (To the girl, with the patience of a tutor for a promising pupil) The stringing, naturally. First light is when the porters came, so you got here with them or before them. Before, I'd wager — no one takes a dead man's boots with porters watching. So: what did you see when you arrived? Was the loft door shut then, as it is now? And what's your name — I dislike addressing walls.

speaker: dice
text: Persuasion check to ask the girl on the wall what she saw when she arrived, whether the loft door was shut, and what her name is: 4 + 0 = 4 vs DC 15: failure

speaker: gm
text:
The girl’s smile sharpens at your patient tone. “I saw him jump at midnight, didn’t I? Wailing about his debts. Moonlight on the whole tragic business.” She looks down at you, waiting to see whether you’ll challenge the embellishment.

From across the yard, Cob chimes in too quickly. “That’s what she said. Cob heard it.” His eyes stay on your face, not the body. The loft door remains shut behind the hanging clerk; the girl gives no name.

speaker: player
text: (I applaud, three slow claps) Charming. Except a man who jumps from a hoist beam at midnight does not first remove his boots, the Sergeant is wearing a rain cape, and Cob's eyes say he's never heard that story before in his life. (I tilt my head at Prout's neck) Sergeant — come and look at this with me. If he hanged himself the rope bruise rides up behind the ears. If someone strangled him and hoisted him after, there's a second line, flat and low. (I step beneath the body and study the throat.)

speaker: dice
text: Medicine check to tell how Prout really died: 19 + 3 = 22 vs DC 12: success

speaker: gm
text:
At the body’s throat, beneath the slanting burn of the noose, you find a second mark: thin, level, and set low. The back of Prout’s skull is swollen under his hair. His palms are clean—no rope burn. The noose did not kill him. Someone struck him, strangled him, then hoisted him up.

Kell comes close enough to see. Her pencil moves across the notebook. “Second cord mark, low and level. Swelling at the back of the skull. No rope burn on the hands.” She reads it back, then looks to you. “Murder, then. Not yet a name.”

On the wall, the girl’s face has gone still. Cob’s stones hang forgotten in his fists.

speaker: player
text: (I turn to the children, and for once I drop the lecturing tone) There. Now you both know what I know: someone cracked his skull and strangled him, then went to the trouble of making it look like grief. A person that careful will want back whatever was hidden in that boot. Cob, you're welcome to the second crown — for a look, as you said, in your own hands, boot stays on. I'd rather you read it to me than have the man who did this come asking you for it.

speaker: gm
text:
Cob’s swagger falters at “the man who did this”; he glances from Prout to the open gate. Moll’s heels stop drumming.

Then Cob holds out his left boot, keeping it firmly on his foot. “Second crown, then. For a look. Boots stay on. No picking, no pulling, no taking.” He takes the coin, but doesn’t offer you the boot.

“Payment for a look. Boots retained by the boy. Noted.” She writes it down. Cob stamps once, and the left boot gives a dry crackle. “There. You’ve had your look.”

marks.note: You offered Cob the second crown for a look while letting him keep the boots. He’s holding you to those terms.
